person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: Taken together, the results of the five experiments support the proposal that behavioral goals can become activated without any consciously made choice required.

span.label: nonconscious goal pursuit
span.quote: Our argument is that goals can be triggered outside of awareness and then run to completion, attaining desired outcomes ( Bargh, 1990 ; Bargh & Chartrand, 1999 ; Bargh & Gollwitzer, 1994 ).

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: Five experiments are reported in which the goal either to perform well or to cooperate was activated, without the awareness of participants, through a priming manipulation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Repeated, consistent pursuit of a goal in a given situation forms an automatic situation-to-goal association, so situational cues alone later activate the goal without conscious choice.
span.quote: In other words, over time the goal representation will develop an automatic association with the features of those situations in which that goal has been repeatedly and consistently chosen and pursued in the past.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An activated but unfulfilled goal-directed action tendency accumulates strength over time (unlike perceptual activation, which decays), which is why the behavioural priming effect grows with delay.
span.quote: Until the goal is acted on, however, the action tendency is posited to increase in strength over time, thus pressing for realization.

span.label: The intention-behaviour correlations rest on small per-cell samples.
span.quote: Because the number of participants on which these correlations are based is somewhat small, these results should be interpreted with caution.

span.label: Retrospective self-report is a weak index of what participants were actually aware of during the task.
span.quote: Nevertheless, it must be acknowledged that any such memory-based self-report measure of prior conscious states is not the most sensitive or powerful measure of actual awareness during the experimental tasks ( Ericsson & Simon, 1980 ).

span.label: The intention questionnaire may not have been sensitive enough to detect real differences in cooperation motivation.
span.quote: However, the lack of a difference between those participants explicitly instructed to cooperate (i.e., the conscious-goal condition) and those not given such instructions raises the issue of whether the intention questionnaire was sufficiently sensitive to capture actual differences in the motivation to cooperate during the task.

span.label: goal pursuit
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption

span.label: content-free features
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption

span.label: persistence
span.quote: In Experiment 4 we addressed the issue of persistence on a task in the face of a clear obstacle to goal attainment. In Experiment 5 we analyzed the issue of resumption of a task after a lengthy disruption has occurred and participants have a chance to switch to an intrinsically more attractive alternative

span.label: resumption
span.quote: In Experiment 4 we addressed the issue of persistence on a task in the face of a clear obstacle to goal attainment. In Experiment 5 we analyzed the issue of resumption of a task after a lengthy disruption has occurred and participants have a chance to switch to an intrinsically more attractive alternative

span.label: perceptual construal
span.quote: No model of priming or accessibility effects on perception or construal predicts an increase in effect over time ( Bargh, 1994 ; Higgins, 1989 , 1996 ; Wyer & Srull, 1989 ). The dissociation we predicted, if goal-priming effects are not mediated by perceptual construal, is straightforward. The effects of the same priming manipulation should decrease over time for a social–perceptual (impression-formation) dependent variable, but they should increase over time for a dependent variable reflecting goal-directed action tendencies

span.label: goal-directed action tendencies
span.quote: No model of priming or accessibility effects on perception or construal predicts an increase in effect over time ( Bargh, 1994 ; Higgins, 1989 , 1996 ; Wyer & Srull, 1989 ). The dissociation we predicted, if goal-priming effects are not mediated by perceptual construal, is straightforward. The effects of the same priming manipulation should decrease over time for a social–perceptual (impression-formation) dependent variable, but they should increase over time for a dependent variable reflecting goal-directed action tendencies

span.label: nonconscious goal pursuit - the claim in one sentence, and note how much is packed into it: goals can be ACTIVATED OUTSIDE OF AWARENESS, then OPERATE nonconsciously, and do so EFFECTIVELY - guiding self-regulation rather than merely biasing a judgement. Three separate assertions (activation without awareness, autonomous operation, functional success), any of which could fail while the others held
span.quote: It is proposed that goals can be activated outside of awareness and then operate nonconsciously to guide self-regulation effectively (J. A. Bargh, 1990 ). Five experiments are reported in which the goal either to perform well or to cooperate was activated, without the awareness of participants, through a priming manipulation

span.label: goal versus construct - THE DISAMBIGUATION THIS CORPUS NEEDS AND RARELY GETS. A prime made of `win, compete, succeed, strive` could have activated a construct that changes how the situation is CONSTRUED, or a goal that DRIVES behaviour. The paper separates them by time course and states the falsifier first: NO model of construal effects predicts an increase over time, so the same prime is required to produce a decreasing perceptual effect and an increasing behavioural one. A crossover, not a difference in size
span.quote: No model of priming or accessibility effects on perception or construal predicts an increase in effect over time ( Bargh, 1994 ; Higgins, 1989 , 1996 ; Wyer & Srull, 1989 ). The dissociation we predicted, if goal-priming effects are not mediated by perceptual construal, is straightforward. The effects of the same priming manipulation should decrease over time for a social–perceptual (impression-formation) dependent variable, but they should increase over time for a dependent variable reflecting goal-directed action tendencies

span.label: DEFINITION BY DIAGNOSTIC SIGNATURE - goal pursuit is identified by CONTENT-FREE features (vigour, persistence against obstacles, resumption after disruption) taken from the study of consciously held goals. Because the criteria are content-free they can be applied to a goal the participant cannot report, which is the only reason the nonconscious version is testable at all. The definition is doing methodological work, not just fixing a meaning
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption

span.label: the control is built into the definition: participants are given ONE AND THE SAME TASK with the goal activated for some and not others, so that `we were able to hold the content of the task goal constant across all participants` and let the content-free features be the only thing that varies. Borrowing a content-free definition and then holding content constant is the same decision made twice, at the level of theory and of design
span.quote: we were able to hold the content of the task goal constant across all participants so that we could examine the content-free features of nonconscious goal pursuit and be able to compare these to the known content-free features of conscious goal pursuit

span.label: replicates → Ovsiankina (1928)
span.quote: This finding replicates the classic finding of Ovsiankina (1928) in the case of conscious goal pursuit.

span.label: builds-on → J. A. Bargh, 1990
span.quote: It is proposed that goals can be activated outside of awareness and then operate nonconsciously to guide self-regulation effectively (J. A. Bargh, 1990 ).

span.label: builds-on → Atkinson and Birch (1970)
span.quote: According to Atkinson and Birch’s (1970) “dynamic theory of action,” goal-directed action tendencies consume their strength to the degree they are acted on, reaching their lowest level of activation immediately after the goal is attained.

span.label: goal pursuit —operationalised-as→ content-free features
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — The definitional move the whole paper rests on. Confidence 0.95: the sentence is a characterisation of goal pursuit, cited to Lewin, Heckhausen and Wicklund & Gollwitzer, not an inference of mine.
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption

span.label: persistence —part-of→ content-free features
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — Listed as one of the three, in the sentence that names the category.
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption

span.label: resumption —part-of→ content-free features
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — The second of the three tested directly - Experiment 5, resumption after a lengthy disruption with a more attractive alternative available.
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption

span.label: goal-directed action tendencies —distinct-from→ perceptual construal
span.note: differs in: WHAT DELAY DOES TO THEM - construal effects DECREASE over time, goal-directed action tendencies INCREASE. A crossover on the same manipulation, and the increase is the half no accessibility or construal model predicts, which is what makes it a falsifier rather than a comparison · strength of the relation: 0.95 — THE SHARPEST ROW ON THIS RECORD. Two kinds of priming effect told apart by their TIME COURSE - the second record tonight where identity turns on latency rather than on magnitude (see Chen2018). The prediction is stated before the experiment and names the result that would refute it.
span.quote: No model of priming or accessibility effects on perception or construal predicts an increase in effect over time ( Bargh, 1994 ; Higgins, 1989 , 1996 ; Wyer & Srull, 1989 ). The dissociation we predicted, if goal-priming effects are not mediated by perceptual construal, is straightforward. The effects of the same priming manipulation should decrease over time for a social–perceptual (impression-formation) dependent variable, but they should increase over time for a dependent variable reflecting goal-directed action tendencies

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: The number of words found by the participants was analyzed by a 2 (prime) × 2 (gender) analysis of variance (ANOVA).

span.label: p-value
span.quote: As predicted, the main effect of prime was reliable, F (1, 74) = 9.64, p = .003.

span.label: interaction effect
span.quote: All of these effects were qualified, however, by the predicted Prime × Delay × Task interaction, F (1, 272) = 5.67, p = .018, which is depicted in Figure 1 .

span.label: t-test
span.quote: Judging the degree of humor of a set series of cartoons ( M = 2.5) was anticipated to be significantly more enjoyable than forming words from Scrabble letter tiles ( M = 1.2), t (18) = 2.32, p < .04.

span.label: Cronbach's alpha
span.quote: When we analyzed participants’ responses to the three postexperimental questions concerning their experienced intentions to cooperate during the task (Cronbach’s α = .74), there were no reliable differences as a function of priming or conscious-goal conditions, all F s < 1.37.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Therefore, to more fully address the relation between the experienced strength of the intention to cooperate and actual cooperative behavior, we computed within-cell correlations between these two measures.

span.label: standardization (z scores)
span.quote: Scores on the performance task (number of words found) and impression-formation task (mean rating of the target person on the three achievement-related scales) were standardized (using z scores) prior to analysis.

span.label: mean
span.quote: Judging the degree of humor of a set series of cartoons ( M = 2.5) was anticipated to be significantly more enjoyable than forming words from Scrabble letter tiles ( M = 1.2), t (18) = 2.32, p < .04.

span.label: Participants primed with high-performance words found more words on unrelated word-search puzzles than participants primed with neutral words.
span.quote: High-performance-goal primed participants found a mean of 26.0 words, compared with a mean of 21.5 words for participants in the neutral priming condition.

span.label: Priming the goal of cooperation increased the number of fish returned to the common pool, as did an explicit conscious cooperation goal.
span.quote: It revealed a main effect for priming, F (1, 56) = 3.93, p = .05, as well as a main effect for conscious goal, F (1, 56) = 5.99, p < .02.

span.label: The goal-priming effect did not depend on a concurrent conscious goal in the same direction, ruling out the 'piggybacking' account.
span.quote: Moreover, in line with our hypothesis that nonconscious-goal activation does not require the preexistence of a conscious goal in the same direction (the piggybacking issue), participants in the no-conscious-goal condition showed the same increase in cooperation due to goal priming as did participants in the conscious-goal condition.

span.label: A five-minute delay after the identical prime weakened the impression-formation (perceptual) effect but strengthened the task-performance (motivational) effect, a crossover dissociation.
span.quote: Most importantly for the present hypotheses, however, primed participants’ achievement-related impressions of the target person became less extreme over time, t (57) = 1.83, p < .04, whereas the performance of primed participants on the word-search task increased over time, t (91) = 2.50, p < .01.

span.label: Performance-goal primed participants were far more likely than neutral-primed participants to keep working after an explicit instruction to stop, showing persistence against an obstacle.
span.quote: A substantially greater proportion of participants in the high-performance–goal priming condition (57%) than in the neutral priming condition (22%) continued to work on the task after the stop signal was given.

span.label: After an interruption, performance-goal primed participants more often resumed the unfinished intellectual task instead of switching to a pretested-more-enjoyable alternative.
span.quote: As predicted, a considerably higher proportion of high-performance–goal primed participants (66%) chose to continue working on die interrupted Scrabble task than did nonprimed participants (32%).

span.label: Self-reported strength of intention predicted behaviour only for consciously held goals, not for primed ones, indicating the priming effect was not mediated by conscious intention.
span.quote: The self-reported intentions of participants with a nonconsciously held goal to cooperate were unrelated to their actual cooperation, even though these participants showed a non-conscious cooperation-goal effect on their behavior.

span.label: automatic (nonconscious) goal pursuit
span.quote: Our argument is that goals can be triggered outside of awareness and then run to completion, attaining desired outcomes ( Bargh, 1990 ; Bargh & Chartrand, 1999 ; Bargh & Gollwitzer, 1994 ).

span.label: content-free features of goal pursuit
span.quote: Goal pursuit (i.e., striving for the desired outcome), however, is also characterized by content-free features, such as vigorous acting toward goal attainment, persistence in the face of obstacles, and resumption after disruption ( Heckhausen, 1991 ; Lewin, 1926 ; Wicklund & Gollwitzer, 1982 ).

span.label: continuing on the task (operational definition of persistence)
span.term: continuing on the task (operational definition of persistence)
span.quote: Continuing on the task was operationally defined as looking for and writing down a new word after the signal

span.label: priming condition (high-performance goal vs. neutral)
span.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to either a high-performance-goal or a neutral priming condition.

span.label: number of words found in the experimental word-search puzzles
span.term: number of words found in the experimental word-search puzzles
span.quote: The dependent variable was the total number of words the participant found in the three experimental word-search puzzles.

span.label: conscious goal condition (none vs. cooperation) and number of fish returned to the lake
span.term: conscious goal condition (none vs. cooperation) and number of fish returned to the lake
span.quote: The design of the study was a 2 (priming: none vs. cooperation) × 2 (conscious goal: none vs. cooperation) between-subjects factorial design, and the dependent measure was the participant’s degree of replenishing the resource, as measured by the number of fish returned to the lake.

span.label: postpriming delay (none vs. 5 min)
span.quote: All of these effects were qualified, however, by the predicted Prime × Delay × Task interaction, F (1, 272) = 5.67, p = .018, which is depicted in Figure 1 .

span.label: task type (impression formation vs. word search)
span.term: task type (impression formation vs. word search)
span.quote: The design was a 2 (priming: high-performance goal vs. control) × 2 (task: impression formation vs. word search) × 2 (delay: none vs. 5 min) × 2 (gender) between-subjects factorial.

span.label: participant gender
span.quote: Gender of participant was included as a factor because, historically, gender differences have often been obtained in the manifestation of achievement orientation—at least as it has been classically operationalized and measured ( Alper, 1974 ; Heckhausen, 1991 , p. 214; Homer, 1972 , 1974 ; Stewart & Chester, 1982 ).

span.label: choice of task after the interruption (resume Scrabble vs. rate cartoons)
span.term: choice of task after the interruption (resume Scrabble vs. rate cartoons)
span.quote: The dependent variable was the participant’s choice of task following the interruption: the Scrabble word-construction task on which they had already started or the objectively more enjoyable cartoon-humor rating task.

span.label: 26.0 vs. 21.5 — mean number of hidden words found by performance-primed versus neutral-primed participants in Experiment 1
span.quote: High-performance-goal primed participants found a mean of 26.0 words, compared with a mean of 21.5 words for participants in the neutral priming condition.

span.label: 57% / 22% — proportion of participants who kept working after the stop signal, performance-primed versus neutral-primed (Experiment 4)
span.quote: A substantially greater proportion of participants in the high-performance–goal priming condition (57%) than in the neutral priming condition (22%) continued to work on the task after the stop signal was given.

span.label: 66% / 32% — proportion who resumed the interrupted Scrabble task rather than switching to the cartoon task, primed versus unprimed (Experiment 5)
span.quote: As predicted, a considerably higher proportion of high-performance–goal primed participants (66%) chose to continue working on die interrupted Scrabble task than did nonprimed participants (32%).

span.label: F (1, 74) = 9.64, p = .003 — the reliable main effect of the performance prime on number of words found in Experiment 1
span.quote: As predicted, the main effect of prime was reliable, F (1, 74) = 9.64, p = .003.

span.label: 78 — number of participants in Experiment 1
span.quote: Seventy-eight introductory psychology students (30 men, 48 women) at New York University (NYU) participated in the experiment in partial fulfillment of a course research requirement.

span.label: 288 — number of participants in the four-factor dissociation study, Experiment 3
span.quote: A total of 288 participants (102 men, 186 women) took part in the experiment in partial fulfillment of a course requirement in an NYU introductory psychology course.

span.label: r = −.11 — the (small, negative) correlation between self-reported intention to cooperate and actual cooperation among participants without a conscious cooperation goal
span.quote: For participants who were not given the conscious goal to cooperate, there was only a small negative relation between self-reported intentions to cooperate and actual amount of cooperation ( r = −.11 overall, −. 16 for no-priming condition, −.10 for goal-priming condition; all p s > .25).
